chunks: Other lithium chemistries and their trade-offs. The question: What are some other common Lithium-based battery chemistries? What are their tradeoffs?
"Lithium-ion" is really a family of batteries, usually named by the material in the positive electrode. Each member trades off energy, lifespan, safety and cost differently.
The skill is matching the right one to the product.
Think of a set of cars from the same maker. One is a fast sports model with a small tank, one a family car that balances everything, and one a slow but nearly unbreakable truck.
They all run on the same basic idea. You pick the one that fits the job.
Lithium cells work the same way: the "engine" is shared, but the electrode material changes the personality.
Representative shapes (not datasheet data). NMC slopes about 8 millivolts per 1% SoC through the middle.
LFP is almost flat from 20% to 80% (about 1 millivolts per 1% SoC), and LTO is flat too, at a much lower voltage. A voltage error of 10 millivolts is about 1.
25% SoC for NMC but about 10% for LFP, which is why LFP gauges need current integration ("Determining state of charge and why it's hard").
Electrode: one of the two sides of a cell that store lithium. The positive one is the cathode, the negative one the anode. Cathode: the positive electrode material.
Its type gives the chemistry its name. LCO / NMC: common cathodes for phones and laptops (LCO) and for tools and electric vehicles (NMC). LFP: lithium iron phosphate.
Safer and long-lived, with lower energy and about 3. 2 volts per cell. LTO: lithium titanate, used for the anode instead of graphite.
Charges very fast and lasts very long, but stores less energy at about 2. 4 volts.
Cycle life: how many charge-discharge cycles before capacity falls to about 80% ("LiPo trade-offs versus other batteries").
Three products, three picks. A phone needs the most energy in the least space, so it uses LCO or NMC.
A backup battery on a wall that cycles daily for years needs safety and long life, so LFP fits.
A bus that fast-charges every stop needs quick charging and huge cycle life, so LTO fits.
Each charger must also match its chemistry, because the full-charge voltage differs (about 4. 2 volts for NMC, about 3. 6 volts for LFP). That is the whole idea.
"Lithium-ion is a family named by the cathode. LCO gives the most energy in a small cell but is the least stable, used in phones.
NMC is the balanced workhorse for tools, e-bikes and EVs. NCA is higher energy still. LMO is cheap and high current but short-lived. LiFePO4 is 3.
2 volts, very safe and thousands of cycles, but lower energy and a flat curve. LTO is about 2. 4 volts, low energy, but charges extremely fast and lasts forever.
Each charges to a different voltage, so match the charger."
